client: I've been really struggling since my partner passed away three months ago. Things I used to love, like going for walks or even just cooking a meal, feel completely pointless now. I'm not sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I should at least try.
therapist: Thank you for being here and for taking that step, even when part of you isn't sure it will help — that kind of courage in the middle of grief is really significant. I notice that as you're describing all of this, there's a heaviness that seems to go even deeper than your words alone, like maybe the weight of it all is harder to carry than you're letting on right now. I'm wondering — when you say things feel pointless, what does a typical moment in your day actually feel like for you on the inside?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Honestly, it's like... I wake up and there's this immediate dread, like before I even fully open my eyes, I already know the day is going to feel empty. I go through the motions, I make coffee, I sit at my desk, but it's like I'm watching myself from a distance and none of it feels real or like it matters. The worst part is there's no one to even talk to about it, so it just kind of sits there inside me, getting heavier.
therapist: What you're describing — that dread before you even open your eyes, the sense of watching your own life from behind glass — sounds absolutely exhausting to carry, especially in the silence of having no one to share it with. It makes so much sense that it keeps getting heavier when there's nowhere for it to go. I'm curious, when you imagine what it might feel like to have that weight *heard* by someone, even just a little — what comes up for you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Honestly, when I try to imagine that... there's this flicker of something, like relief maybe, but it gets swallowed up almost immediately by this fear that whoever's listening would just get tired of it. Like, I've had people in my life before who seemed like they cared, and then at some point I could just feel them pulling away, and that almost made things worse than if I'd never said anything at all. So now there's this part of me that thinks it's just safer to keep it to myself, even though keeping it to myself is also slowly suffocating me.
therapist: What you just described is such a painful bind — reaching out feels risky, but staying silent is slowly crushing you, and you've been hurt before by people who couldn't hold the weight of your pain. That fear of being too much for someone, of watching them pull away, makes complete sense given what you've experienced. I want you to know that noticing that flicker of relief — even for just a moment — tells me that part of you is still reaching toward connection, and I think that part is worth listening to.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Yeah, I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that... but it also feels kind of naive, like that flicker of relief is just wishful thinking rather than something real I can actually act on. Every time I've let myself hope that someone could handle what I'm carrying, it's ended with me feeling more alone than before. I guess I'm just not sure how to trust that instinct when it's gotten me hurt so many times.
therapist: The way you're describing this — calling hope "naive" — sounds like a protection strategy your mind has built after being hurt, and honestly, given your history, that makes a lot of sense. But I'm struck by something: you're still here, still talking, still noticing that flicker, which suggests that part of you hasn't fully given up on the idea that connection could be different. What do you think it would take — even just the smallest thing — for that instinct toward hope to feel a little safer to trust?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess... yeah, maybe you're right that it's some kind of protection thing. But even hearing you say "it could be different" makes me tense up, because I've told myself that before and then ended up feeling even more stupid when it didn't work out. I think what it would take is some kind of proof that the risk is actually worth it, but I don't even know how you'd get that without just... getting hurt again first.
therapist: You've just named something really profound — that the only way to get proof of safety is to risk the very thing that's hurt you before, and that feels like an impossible catch-22. I notice there's something almost tender in the way you're wrestling with this, like underneath the wariness there's still a part of you that *wants* to be wrong about people. What if, instead of looking for proof all at once, we got curious together about what the smallest, most manageable step toward trust might look like — one where the stakes feel a little less like everything?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I mean... yeah, you're right that there's a part of me that wants to be wrong about people. That's almost embarrassing to admit out loud. But when you say "smallest step," I honestly don't even know what that looks like anymore, because even tiny things have blown up in my face before and left me feeling more alone than if I'd just stayed closed off.
therapist: There's nothing embarrassing about wanting to be wrong about people — that's actually one of the most human things you've said, and it takes real courage to admit it. I also want to gently hold what you just shared, that even small steps have left you more alone, because that's important — it means we're not looking for a step that requires you to trust someone else first, but maybe something that starts with you and what *you* need. I'm wondering, in those moments after things "blew up," what was it that hurt the most — was it the other person's reaction, or something you told yourself about what it meant?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Honestly, both hurt, but if I'm being real... it was mostly what I told myself after. Like, the other person would get frustrated or pull away, and then my brain would immediately go to "see, this is proof that you're too much, that you always ruin things." It's like their reaction was just the trigger, but I was the one who really did the damage with everything I said to myself afterward.
therapist: What you just uncovered is really significant — that the story your mind told you afterward, "you're too much, you always ruin things," was doing far more damage than the other person's reaction ever could. That voice sounds like it's been with you for a long time, and I'm curious whether it showed up even before the losses and disappointments, or whether grief has made it louder.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That question actually stopped me for a second, because I think... yeah, it was there before. Even as a kid I remember feeling like I took up too much space, like I needed to shrink myself down so people wouldn't get tired of me. But losing my dad and then my closest friend moving away, it's like those things just confirmed what the voice was already whispering.
therapist: What you just traced is so important — that voice telling you that you're "too much" didn't start with loss, it started long before, and then life handed you experiences that felt like confirmation of something you'd already been told to believe about yourself. There's something that strikes me about the way you're describing this, though — like you're moving through it quickly, almost matter-of-factly, and I wonder if underneath that there's something that still feels really tender or painful about that little kid who learned to shrink. What comes up for you when you sit with that image for a moment?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I mean... yeah, I guess I do move through it fast. It's kind of easier to just explain it like it's a story that happened to someone else, like I'm reading off a timeline. But when you say "that little kid"... I don't know, something kind of tightens in my chest, like I don't really want to go there.
therapist: That tightening in your chest is worth paying attention to — it's like your body is telling you something that the "timeline" version of the story keeps at a safe distance. The fact that you noticed it, and named it, even while part of you wants to move away from it, feels like a really honest moment. I don't want to push you somewhere you're not ready to go, but I'm curious — when you feel that tightening, what's the first word or image that comes to mind, even if it doesn't quite make sense?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: The first word that comes to mind is "invisible." Like, when I feel that tightening, there's this image of me sitting at a table with people around me, talking and laughing, and I'm right there but nobody's actually seeing me. It doesn't fully make sense because I'm not literally alone, but that's what hits me when I sit with it.
therapist: "Invisible" — that word carries so much, and that image of being surrounded by people but unseen is one of the loneliest feelings there is, maybe even lonelier than being physically alone. It makes complete sense that this connects back to that little kid who learned to shrink, because invisibility can start to feel like the price of belonging — like you can be *near* people, but only if you don't take up too much space. I'm wondering if that's part of what's been happening with grief too — like losing your partner didn't just take them, it took the one person who maybe made you feel truly visible?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
